"Literally" means: exactly as stated, in the real world, not as a figure of speech.

When you use "literally," you are telling your listener: "This is exactly what happened. Don't interpret it loosely. Don't read it as an exaggeration or a metaphor. I mean it word for word, fact for fact."
The Most Important Contrast: Literally vs. Figuratively

To truly understand "literally," you must understand what it stands against — its opposite: figuratively.

Figuratively means you are using words to paint a picture or create a feeling, but not meaning them as exact fact. It's an image, a dramatic expression, a way of speaking.

Literally means you mean exactly what the words say. No poetic license. No exaggeration. The real thing.

Here is a side-by-side look at the same idea, expressed both ways:

  • "I was so scared, my heart stopped." → Figurative. Your heart didn't actually stop. You're using dramatic language to express deep fear.
  • "The doctor said my heart literally stopped for two seconds during the surgery." → Literal. Your heart actually, physically, in real life stopped. The organ stopped beating.

Notice the difference? The figurative version is about feeling. The literal version is about fact.
More Examples of the Correct Use

• "The book says to add three cups of water. Do it literally."
    Follow the instruction exactly. Not roughly three cups. Not about two and a half. Exactly three.
  • "She literally ran a marathon yesterday."
    She actually ran 26.2 miles in real life, with her own feet, on a real course.
  • "The building literally collapsed."
    The structure actually, physically fell down. Not "it felt like it was falling apart." It fell.
  • "I was so tired, I literally fell asleep mid-sentence."
    You actually, genuinely fell asleep while speaking. This really happened.

In each of these cases, "literally" is doing a specific job: it is anchoring the statement in reality. It's saying: "This is not poetry. This is not dramatization. This is a real event, a real fact."
When and Why People Use It

People use "literally" when they worry the listener might think they're exaggerating or speaking figuratively. Saying "literally" pre-empts that misunderstanding.

Imagine you say: "I waited for ages." Your friend might think you're just being dramatic — maybe you waited five minutes. But if you say: "I literally waited for two hours," you are insisting: no, this is not an exaggeration. Two hours actually passed.

So "literally" acts like a signal that says: "Take this at face value. I am not being poetic."
The Modern Informal Use (and Why It Confuses People)

Here is where things get interesting — and a little ironic.

In everyday speech (especially among younger people, and widely on the internet), "literally" is very commonly used in a completely opposite way — as a word that simply adds emphasis or intensity, even when the thing being described is clearly not literal.

  • "I literally died laughing."
    You did not die. You are alive, reading this. But people say this to express that something was extremely funny.
  • "She is literally the most amazing person I have ever met."
    Used for strong emphasis, not to distinguish from a figurative claim.
  • "I literally cannot even."
    A common expression of exasperation or overwhelm, with no literal meaning at all.

This use — where "literally" functions as an intensifier (a word that just makes the feeling stronger, like "very," "absolutely," or "so") — is now so widespread that dictionaries like Merriam-Webster and Oxford have formally added it as an accepted definition.
Why This Informal Use Feels Contradictory

Language purists and grammar enthusiasts often point out the irony: "literally" was designed to mean "this is not figurative," yet it is now routinely used to intensify figurative statements.

"I literally died" — when you say this, you are using a word that means "this really happened in the exact sense," to describe something that literally did not happen (you didn't die). It is, in a way, the word canceling its own meaning.

This is why the word sparks debate. But the debate is largely settled in practical terms: both uses are now recognized and understood.
How to Think About It: Two Lives of the Same Word

To keep this clear in your mind, think of "literally" as living two lives:

Life 1 — Formal/Precise use:
"Literally" means in a factual, exact sense; not figuratively.
This is its original and technically accurate meaning.
Use this in writing, professional settings, or when you want to make a precise factual claim.

Life 2 — Informal/Spoken use:
"Literally" functions as a word of strong emphasis, like "absolutely" or "totally."
This is its modern, colloquial meaning.
Most people use this in casual conversation, and audiences understand it perfectly well — even though, technically, it's the opposite of what the word was built to mean.
A Practical Guide: When to Use It and When to Avoid It

Use "literally" (formal sense) when:

  • You want to make clear that something actually happened, and you're worried the listener might take it as an exaggeration.
  • You want to draw a sharp contrast with a figurative expression.
  • You're translating or following instructions, and you want to signal strict, word-for-word fidelity. (Example: "Translate this paragraph literally.")

Avoid "literally" when:

  • The thing you're describing clearly did not happen in reality. In formal writing, this would look like a mistake.
  • You're in a professional, academic, or formal context — readers may judge the emphatic informal use as careless.

In casual speech:
Feel free to use it the way most people around you use it. Your listeners will understand, because this use is now deeply embedded in everyday English.

The word "literally" does one core thing: it insists on reality. It tells your listener: "Strip away any dramatic flair. Take the words at face value. This is exactly what happened."

Whether you use it in the formal sense (to confirm something really occurred) or the modern informal sense (to add emotional force), understanding that core mission — insisting on realness — will help you grasp every use of this word you'll ever encounter.
